standard.title: Evaluate solutions against criteria and future impact
standard.description: evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria, user stories, possible future impact and opportunities for enterprise
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria, user stories and sustainability (AC9TDI8P10). They have experience applying criteria-based evaluation. They have not yet evaluated for future impact, unintended consequences of AI systems, or enterprise/pivot opportunities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate existing and student solutions against design criteria, user stories, possible future impact (including unintended consequences) and opportunities for enterprise.

nodes.label: Evaluating against design criteria and user stories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate a digital solution by judging its quality against specific design criteria and user stories.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate a solution against at least two design criteria; state clearly whether each criterion is met and provide evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate a solution systematically against all design criteria and user stories; for each criterion, provide evidence of whether it is met; identify areas where the solution partially meets criteria and explain what would be needed to fully meet them.
wider: Evaluate an existing product (e.g. a safety by design implementation in a social media platform) against criteria derived from the Safety by Design Vision — identify where it meets and fails to meet each criterion
Evaluate a student solution with a peer using shared criteria — compare independent evaluations and resolve disagreements about whether criteria are met

response_modes.reason: Evaluation requires evidence-based reasoning against criteria, not subjective opinion. Students without structure often evaluate by feel. A scaffold — criterion → evidence for → evidence against → judgement — produces defensible evaluations.

success_criteria: Each criterion is assessed with specific evidence (not just yes/no)
Evaluation distinguishes between fully met, partially met and not met criteria
nodes.hinge_reason: Evidence-based criteria evaluation at N1 is prerequisite for N2 — identifying unintended consequences requires the same structured analytical approach; students who evaluate by preference produce consequence analysis that is similarly ungrounded.

nodes.label: Evaluating future impact and unintended consequences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate a digital solution's possible future impact, including unintended consequences, and explain how design choices affect downstream outcomes.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one possible unintended consequence of a digital solution and explain how the design decision contributed to it.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate a digital solution's future impact — including intended benefits, possible unintended consequences, and how the design could be changed to mitigate negative impacts; consider impacts on diverse user populations.
wider: Examine how AI image generation solutions trained on homogeneous data produce outputs that fail to represent diverse users — explain the training data decision that caused this and what would mitigate it
Analyse the complexities of training predictive models on low-probability events (e.g. autonomous vehicle edge cases) and evaluate how solution design should account for these
Evaluate a solution's data privacy implications over time — what data is collected, retained, and what could be done with it beyond the original purpose

response_modes.reason: Unintended consequences are abstract without real-world cases. AI bias, autonomous vehicle edge cases, and privacy creep each illuminate a different category of future impact — together they build a more complete framework for impact assessment than any single example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: AI training bias and low-probability edge cases are both substantive and consequential directions — they require students to think about deployment-time failure modes that aren't visible during development, which is genuinely sophisticated thinking.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one unintended consequence of the solution
Connects the consequence to a specific design decision or data choice
Suggests at least one change that would mitigate the identified consequence

nodes.label: Evaluating for enterprise and pivot opportunities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how existing products have met the needs of different user groups and identify opportunities for enterprise or solution adaptation.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of a digital product that has adapted to meet the needs of a different user group; explain what changed and what user need it addressed.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate how existing products have pivoted to meet the needs of different users (e.g. how social media applications have expanded the types of media and interactions); identify what made the pivot possible and what new user needs it addressed.
wider: Identify an unmet user need in an existing product category and propose how a solution could be adapted or extended to address it — evaluate the feasibility of the adaptation
Examine how platforms that began with one user group have expanded (positively or negatively) to serve others — evaluate the design changes that enabled this
success_criteria: Identifies a specific product adaptation and the user need it addressed
Explains what changed in the product to serve the new user group
